t: Guarani is a Tupian language that Paraguay kept: where people across the Americas shifted to the colonial languages, Paraguayans held on to Guarani while also adopting Spanish.

Jesuit missionaries first wrote it down, in grammars and a dictionary of 1629–1640; the Guarani of their missions built new words from its own roots, while the Guarani spoken outside took in Spanish words freely.
Banned from Paraguay’s state schools for over a hundred years, yet used by populists to stir national feeling, it was made equal to Spanish in the constitution of 1992.
dyk: Guarani marks time on nouns as well as verbs: tetã ruvichakue is “ex-president” and tetã ruvicharã “president-elect”, and pa'irãgue, “the ex-future priest”, is someone who studied for the priesthood but did not finish.
ev: The Jesuit Alonso de Aragona completes a teaching grammar of Guarani, not printed until 1979
Antonio Ruiz de Montoya produces the Tesoro de la Lengua Guaraní, the first dictionary of its kind
Ruiz de Montoya’s Arte de la lengua Guaraní becomes the starting point for all later grammars of the language
The Jesuits are expelled, and the people of the reductions move towards Asunción, where the mission Guarani gives way to the everyday Guarani of Paraguay
Paraguay’s new democratic constitution makes Guarani a language equal to Spanish
Guarani becomes the second official language of the Argentine province of Corrientes
The Brazilian town of Tacuru adopts Guarani as a co-official language
Only 12% of Paraguayans now speak Guarani alone, against 28% in 2002, while Spanish monolingualism has not risen

f.family: Tupian: the Tupi–Guarani branch; Paraguayan Guarani is part of a dialect chain, most of whose varieties are also called Guarani
f.script: The Latin alphabet, since the Jesuit grammars and dictionary of 1629–1640; the letter y writes the vowel ɨ
f.earliest: The Jesuit Alonso de Aragona’s teaching grammar, completed in 1629 (printed in 1979); Antonio Ruiz de Montoya’s dictionary, the Tesoro de la Lengua Guaraní (1639), and grammar, the Arte de la lengua Guaraní (1640)
f.status: Living: more than four million speakers in Paraguay, Bolivia, Brazil and Argentina; official in Paraguay beside Spanish (equal to it since the 1992 constitution), in Bolivia and in the Argentine province of Corrientes, and one of the three official languages of Mercosur; rated “vulnerable” by UNESCO
